newsitem.title: GERMANY: European filmmakers brim with new-found confidence.
newsitem.headline: European filmmakers brim with new-found confidence.

text.p: European film makers who once screamed loudly for government protection against the invasion from Hollywood have quietly dropped their cries for quotas and discovered an easier way to win audiences -- make better films.

After years of acrimonious confrontation with the American film industry, which had grabbed an astonishing 80 percent or more of their local film markets, many European filmmakers have turned their venom into vigour.

Borrowing ideas and techniques on producing and marketing from Hollywood, film makers in Britain, Germany, France, Spain and elsewhere have shifted their focus onto making commercially successful films that please vast audiences rather than dull auteur films made principally to satisfy the director.

This new-found confidence has been on abundant display at this year's Berlin Film Festival, which runs to February 24. Film makers from many European countries have been brimming with optimism over rising domestic interest in their films.

"The war between Europe and America is over," said Berlinale director Moritz de Hadeln in an interview with Reuters. "The enormous presence of American films in the European market has made people think 'if the American films are so successful, why can't we make films like that too?'."

Whether a German romantic comedy, a British period piece or a French family drama, the home audiences are coming back. At least three German, French and Spanish films were in the top 10 of their respective domestic box office charts last week.

The fact that three of the five Academy Awards nominations announced last week in Los Angeles for best actress and best film went to European productions such as "The English Patient" and "Secrets and Lies" added to the era of good feeling.

The British war-time romance "The English Patient", favoured to reap a rich harvest of Oscars after picking up 12 nominations, had been rejected by many Hollywood studios. The film should win the Berlinale's "Golden Bear" for best film.

"There is much more confidence in Europe now," de Hadeln said. "We have learned many lessons from the Americans about how to do things and how not to do things. We are finding subjects that appeal to audiences of different cultures. We are making better films. The animosity is gone. There is no reason to fear the Americans."

In Germany, the world's second largest film market with 1.33 billion marks in ticket sales last year, German films grabbed 17 percent of their home market last year, the highest level in three decades and double the figure for 1995.

"There has been a big change in the outlook," said German producer Bernd Eichinger. "The public was always there, but we did not deliver the right product. The public is regaining confidence in filmmakers, and the filmmakers have regained their faith in the audiences."
While it is impossible to speak of a single European market, the respective national film industries are clearly having more success in standing up to Hollywood.

Another important trend, film industry executives say, is the effort by producers such as Eichinger to make some big-budget films in English even if they are set in Germany, France, Denmark or elsewhere.

"If the film is English, even if it is grounded in Germany or France or some wherever, it will have a greater value than if it is not," said Thomas Garvin, a Hollywood film lawyer. "But the 'Europudding' trash grounded nowhere has no chance."

Many of those were set somewhere in Europe, but had an indistinguishable international flavour and often such weak storylines that they seemed to be written more for the benefit of European Union subsidy boards than any audience.

The Europeans are still clearly reliant on millions of government subsidies. About $500 million in EU and national public money is poured into their production, but the increasing importance of private funding has helped focus attention on making economically viable productions.

"Smilla's Sense of Snow", a German-Danish co-production that opened the Berlinale, is an example of the emerging trend. Eichinger raised $35 million for the English-language film that stars Julia Ormond and Richard Harris.
Released in Germany after the world premiere here, the film set in Denmark shot to the top of Germany's box office charts, knocking the American film "Space Jam" off the top.
